The dwarf little fruit bat (Rhinophylla pumilio) is a small phyllostomid species inhabiting lowland tropical forests of the Amazon basin. Neonates emerge weighing approximately 3.9 grams [Wwb = approximately 3.9 grams], a modest birth mass characteristic of altricial mammals reliant on extended maternal care. Field observations indicate that females typically produce a single pup per litter [N_R_i = single pup per litter] and, under the thermal conditions typical of their active thermoregulatory state, maintain an annual reproductive frequency of roughly one litter per year [F_R_i = roughly one litter per year] at a core body temperature of 34.7 °C [T = 34.7 °C]. This synchronized reproductive output aligns with seasonal fruit abundance in the understory, where the species primarily forages on figs and other small berries. Comparisons with other members of the Carolliinae subfamily suggest that Rhinophylla pumilio has evolved a relatively conservative reproductive strategy, with the single-pup litter representing a widespread pattern among small Neotropical frugivores. The pup, born with closed eyes and sparse pelage, remains in the roost while the mother forages nocturnally, returning periodically to nurse.

During the early post-natal period, the neonate grows rapidly while remaining entirely dependent on lactation. Weaning occurs approximately 30.5 days after birth [tx = approximately 30.5 days after birth] at a core body temperature of 34.7 °C [T = 34.7 °C], marking the transition to nutritional independence. At this juncture, the juvenile attains a wet body mass of about 8 grams [Wwx = about 8 grams], reflecting substantial somatic growth from the initial neonatal weight. The timing of weaning is tightly linked to the ripening phenology of key fruit resources, as the newly independent young must successfully locate and process solid food items. Field studies in Peruvian lowland forests indicate that weaning coincides with peaks in Ficus availability, ensuring a reliable food supply for the vulnerable young. Following nutritional emancipation, the juvenile continues to refine its foraging skills, gradually expanding its home range while remaining loosely associated with the maternal roost for several additional weeks before dispersing to establish an independent territory.

Gestation in Rhinophylla pumilio extends for approximately 106 days [tg = approximately 106 days] at a body temperature of 34.7 °C [T = 34.7 °C], a relatively prolonged developmental period given the species' small body size. This extended gestation is thought to reflect the energetic constraints imposed by a diet of low-protein fruits, which may limit the rate of foetal tissue accretion. Embryogenesis proceeds through the typical eutherian sequence, with organogenesis largely completed during the first half of gestation. The gravid female maintains a stable thermal regime throughout pregnancy, and the core temperature of 34.7 °C [T = 34.7 °C] appears critical for normal foetal development. Unlike some phyllostomids that exhibit delayed implantation or embryonic diapause, Rhinophylla pumilio undergoes continuous gestation from fertilization to parturition. Reproductive females captured during the late dry season consistently show advanced foetal development, suggesting that the timing of mating is aligned with the subsequent peak in fruit availability, thereby ensuring optimal nutritional conditions for the lactating mother and her dependent offspring.

Sexual maturation in this species occurs relatively late for a bat of its stature. Puberty is reached at 120 days after birth [tp = 120 days after birth] at a body temperature of 34.7 °C [T = 34.7 °C], indicating that individuals require several months of post-weaning growth before achieving reproductive competence. The onset of gonadal activity is marked by testicular descent in males and the first ovulation in females, events that coincide with the attainment of near-adult body dimensions. Males frequently achieve a maximum adult wet body mass of 9.4 grams [Wwi = 9.4 grams], while females can attain a slightly larger ultimate wet body mass of 10.4 grams [Wwi = 10.4 grams], a modest sexual size dimorphism typical of species where males engage in non-aggressive courtship displays. The slightly larger female size may confer advantages in terms of foetal accommodation and lactation energetics. Radio-tracking studies have documented that newly mature individuals quickly establish foraging territories and may breed during their first year, contributing to the species' relatively high population turnover in undisturbed habitats.

Basal metabolic rate measurements conducted under standard respirometric protocols reveal a resting oxygen consumption of 18.6 milliliters per hour [JOi = 18.6 milliliters per hour] at a core body temperature of 34.7 °C [T = 34.7 °C]. This metabolic rate is consistent with values reported for other small frugivorous bats and reflects the energetic demands of a high-surface-area-to-volume ratio. Maximum recorded longevity in the wild reaches approximately 13 years [am = approximately 13 years] at 34.7 °C [T = 34.7 °C], indicating that despite its small size, Rhinophylla pumilio exhibits a relatively slow pace of life compared to similarly-sized insectivorous species. The combination of a low reproductive rate—a single pup annually—and an extended lifespan suggests a life-history strategy oriented toward adult survival rather than high fecundity, an adaptation well suited to the stable but resource-limited environment of Neotropical evergreen forests. Senescence-related mortality becomes apparent after approximately a decade, with older individuals showing reduced foraging efficiency and increased ectoparasite loads before natural death occurs.
